title: The Banyan Deer King
text:
The king of Benares loved hunting deer so much that he forced his subjects to leave their fields to drive game for him. To free themselves, the people built a great enclosure in the royal park and herded two whole herds of deer into it. One herd was led by the Banyan Deer, the future Buddha, and the other by the Branch Deer. The king spared both leaders but hunted the rest, and many deer were wounded in the chase.

To end the needless suffering, the two deer kings agreed that each day one deer would go by lot to the chopping block, taken in turn from each herd. One day the lot fell on a pregnant doe from the Branch Deer's herd. She asked to wait until her fawn was born, but her leader refused. She went to the Banyan Deer, who told her to go back to her herd. Then he walked to the block himself and laid his head on it.

The cook ran to the king, who came and asked why the deer king he had spared was there. The Banyan Deer explained. The king, moved, granted life to him and the doe. The Banyan Deer then asked for the same for the rest of the deer, and step by step for all four-footed creatures, birds and fish, until the king had granted protection to all of them.
lesson: Rules that sacrifice the weakest are easy to accept until someone with standing refuses to. A leader willing to take the cost personally can change what those above him consider normal.
people: The Bodhisatta as the Banyan Deer king, the Branch Deer, a pregnant doe, the king of Benares
